Summarise a fitted FINN model

Source: R/xAI.R
summary.finn_class.Rd

Collects what is needed to judge a fitted model, in this order:

  1. Skill: per response, R2 (1 - SSE/SST) and the correlation (Pearson r) of observed and simulated first, then RMSE, the bias, the ratio of the mean prediction to the mean observation (is the magnitude right?; for mortality weighted by the trees at risk, where the observations carry n_at_risk and n_died) and n; for mortality also the tree-level AUC and the ratio of predicted to observed deaths. On the training data and, when evaluate() or the argument holdout of fit() stored one, on the holdout. The observations are compared with the simulation aggregated the way fit() scores it (see comparePlot()). Without a stored evaluation, summary() runs evaluate() on the training data first (one simulation) and stores it on the model.

  2. Convergence: by how many percent each loss term changed over the last epochs_back epochs (the mean of the last epochs_back epochs against the mean of the epochs_back before), as a table with one sentence on the largest change; and how much the parameters moved over the last epochs_back epochs, as a table with one row per process (growth, mortality, regeneration, competition) and part (its species parameters, where they are fitted (optimizeSpecies = TRUE in createProcess()), its environmental response, i.e. the network or the linear climate effects, and for regeneration the recruit dispersion and the cap), naming the parameter that moved most. The change is the size of the step the values took as a percentage of their size, 100 * |values now - values then| / |values then|, over all species of a parameter (on the scale it acts on, e.g. "mortality: growth") or all weights of a network layer; 1 % means the values moved by about a hundredth of their size. fit() keeps the parameters of the last 51 epochs for this, so epochs_back can be at most 50; for a model fitted before this version the parameter snapshots of the fit (model$param_history, every checkpoints epochs) are used instead; they carry no epoch, so the epochs between them are estimated from the length of the loss history and their number (exact for one call of fit() whose epochs is a multiple of checkpoints). Below the explanation, one sentence names the species parameter that moved most and the largest change overall. A fit has settled when both are small; network weights can keep moving while the loss stays flat.

  3. Bare ground, when evaluate() stored a bare-ground run: per site, the total basal area and the leading species with its share, as the mean over the last tenth of the run.

  4. Environmental importance and average conditional effects, per process and species, from the model's conditional effects (computed once and cached, see ALE()). Where they cannot be computed for a model, a warning says why and the other sections are still returned.

print() shows it; print(s, epochs_back = 10) redoes the convergence check over another window without recomputing anything. plot.finn_class() draws the fitted parameters themselves.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'finn_class'
summary(
  object,
  env = NULL,
  init_cohort = NULL,
  importance = c("ale", "permutation"),
  env_autoscale = TRUE,
  sim_seed = 42L,
  nperm = 20L,
  scale = TRUE,
  epochs_back = 50L,
  ...,
  species_names = NULL,
  parameter_names = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'summary.finn_class'
print(x, epochs_back = x$epochs_back, species = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

object

(finn_class)
fitted model.

env, init_cohort

(NULL or data)
interpretation data for the importance and the conditional effects; NULL uses the cached training data (see ALE()).

importance

(character(1))
"ale" (default) = analytical ALE-variance importance (cheap, from the cache); "permutation" = re-simulating permutation importance (see feature_importance()), cached on the model under the same input key.

env_autoscale

(logical(1))
see ALE().

sim_seed

(integer(1))
seed for the simulation (see ALE()).

nperm

(integer(1))
replicates for importance = "permutation".

scale

(logical(1))
for importance = "ale", divide Var(ALE) by the process x species rate variance so the importances are dimensionless and comparable across processes and species (Sobol-style). Default TRUE.

epochs_back

(integer(1))
the window of the convergence check, in epochs. Default 50.

...

summary(): passed to feature_importance() with importance = "permutation" (and from there to predict()). print(): unused.

species_names, parameter_names

Names of the species and of the parameters of a process function of one's own, as for plot.finn_class(); NULL (default): the species names the model keeps from fit() and the documented parameter names of FINN's own process functions.

x

A summary.finn_class object.

species

(logical(1))
also print the skill per species. Default FALSE.

Value

summary(): an object of class summary.finn_class, a list with skill (per set, overall), skill_species (per set and species), convergence (the loss history, the recent parameters, the parameter snapshots with their estimated spacing, and the bounds and names of the species parameters), bare_ground, importance, average_conditional_effects, method (the importance option), importance_label, species_names, environment_error (NULL, or why item 4 could not be computed) and epochs_back. print(): x, invisibly.

See also

evaluate(), comparePlot(), plot.finn_class(), ALE(), averageConditionalEffects(), feature_importance()

Examples

library(data.table)
# a small model fitted on two Oregon FIA sites (see ?fit)
sites <- 1:2
Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species)
init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp)
FINN.seed(1)
m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
          growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),
          mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),
          regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped))
fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],
    init_cohort = init, epochs = 3L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
    plot_progress = FALSE)
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00301, ba=8.77, trees=0.852, growth=1.58e+04, mortality=32.4, regeneration=0.677)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%

s <- summary(m)
#> Evaluating on the training data (one simulation); evaluate() can add a holdout and a bare-ground run.
s
